Lessons.Title: Plot and Label Points
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM K5 2021 U07:L02 introduces ordered pairs (x,y) and distinguishes the horizontal first coordinate and vertical second coordinate. Exact source first-quadrant POINTS and their drawn axes must be preserved.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder A Point uses original single plotted point from publisher image. Its coordinate values are not independently visible in teacher HTML, so teacher verifies actual image rather than inventing a marked point.

Activity1 What's the Point is a TWO-ROUND hidden card partner exercise. Partner A chooses source point card, verbally describes and partner B plots, compares original publisher card with drawing, and revises precision. Actual card coordinates not independently verified. Student-facing activity does not reduce to a numeric answer.

Activity2 Plot and Label Points original source A/B/C must be READ FROM ORIGINAL PRINTED GRID, whose numeric label content is embedded in artwork; do not fabricate their coordinates. It does explicitly list D=(6,4),E=(2,5),F=(8,3) for students to plot. For these exact points F is farthest right, E highest, and D lies at x6,y4. Source x/y reversal is a meaningful error.

Selected Practice covers source D/E/F ordered pairs and coordinate component checks only; peer card descriptions, A/B/C picture decoding, actual plotting and gated source Cool-down need TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Independent exit ticket uses separate coordinates.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: use ordered pairs to plot and label points in the FIRST quadrant and communicate the location clearly with a partner, correcting the common reversal of horizontal and vertical coordinates. The source starts with a two-round hidden-point description game and peer revision before independent plotting.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: compare point (3,4) with (4,3) on one numbered coordinate grid. The coordinates use the same digits but describe different locations. Trace from (0,0) along the horizontal x-axis first and then vertically to the required y-coordinate; label both axes and scale.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — original point guessing: one student privately chooses one point from (2,5),(5,2),(4,4),(6,1); the partner asks precise location questions and plots the answer. After two rounds each partner writes and revises a mathematical description using 'four units right, then four units up' style language. A numeric answer alone does not certify the drawn point or communication.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — map coordinates: place D=(6,4), E=(2,5), F=(8,3) on a first-quadrant grid with unit tick marks. Explain why F has the largest horizontal coordinate while E has the highest vertical coordinate; review an incorrect plotting of (2,5) as (5,2) and correct it.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: physical plotting, labels, scale, partner questions and revised explanations need teacher review. An exact ordered-pair string is a subcheck only and cannot replace a source workbook coordinate-grid drawing.

KeyConcepts.Title: Ordered pair convention
KeyConcepts.Definition: First coordinate is horizontal x; second is vertical y.

KeyConcepts.Title: First-quadrant scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Positive unit marks on both axes identify positions.
KeyConcepts.Example: Every grid step must use a consistent unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Precise communication
KeyConcepts.Definition: A point description must identify the horizontal and vertical movement, rather than vague 'high/right'.
KeyConcepts.Example: Ask a partner to re-create the point.

Lessons.Title: Points on the Coordinate Plane
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM K5 2021 Grade5 U07:L03 extends the coordinate grid to points sharing one coordinate and to points lying ON the horizontal/vertical axes where one coordinate equals zero. Numeric point location is assessed along with actual student plotting and explanation.
Warm-up Notice and Wonder Points with Zero includes original source picture; students explain why one coordinate being0 does NOT mean an undefined point, it means one axis of the coordinate plane.

Activity1 What's the Point printed Partner A: A(5,1),B(5,2),C(5,3),D(5,4), which are vertically aligned at x5, plus(5,0) on horizontal axis. Partner B: A(4,3),B(5,3),C(6,3),D(7,3), horizontally aligned at y3, plus(0,3) on vertical axis. These actual source positions are recorded precisely.

Activity2 Plotting Points Without a Grid has a source point shown on an axes-only figure whose exact numeric coordinates cannot be certified from text alone; asks students to plot points and determine whether (1,0) and(0,1) can be placed ACCURATELY. Scale must be justified from given visual reference; do not assert a picture shows a unique tick spacing unless verified.

Selected exact Practice validates printed coordinate labels and axes only, not the freehand graphs and teacher discussion. Previous correct invented diagram examples remain optional Edulytiks extensions and original gated source Cool-down is separately unverified.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: recognize that points sharing x lie vertically aligned and points sharing y lie horizontally aligned, including points on coordinate AXES. The source asks students to estimate location before using a fully marked grid and to infer unit scale from a single known point on a blank plane.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: predict the positions of (5,1),(5,2),(5,3),(5,4) without drawing: all are at x=5 and form a vertical line, while (4,3),(5,3),(6,3),(7,3) form a horizontal line at y=3. Check your prediction by plotting.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — axes and estimates: mark (5,0) on x-axis and (0,3) on y-axis. Explain why a zero coordinate means the point lies ON an axis, not that it is missing. In a blank grid with only point (4,2), infer an original unit interval, find (4,0) and (0,2), then explain how (1,0) and (0,1) can be located with reliable axis scale.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — point patterns: partner A plots points with x fixed at 6 and y=1,3,5; partner B plots points with y fixed at2 and x=1,4,7. Compare vertical and horizontal alignment, make one accurate drawing for each, and write the constant coordinate in words.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: selecting scale and plotting on a BLANK coordinate plane are source-core mathematical skills, requiring actual figure inspection and student explanation. An array of point strings is not sufficient authenticated rendering parity.

KeyConcepts.Definition: All (a,y) points have same horizontal distance from y-axis.

KeyConcepts.Title: Zero coordinate places an axis point
KeyConcepts.Definition: For (x,0), point lies on x-axis; (0,y) lies on y-axis.

Lessons.Title: Patterns and Relationships
ExplanationParagraphs: Original Grade5 U07:L09 Generate Patterns gives TWO recursively defined numerical sequences starting at zero, with one addend multiple of the other, and asks pupils to find far-away CORRESPONDING terms rather than merely listing early entries.
Warm-up Choral Count Two Patterns is a public counting routine whose source student numbers arise from classroom contributions and teacher pacing; actual oral turns require teacher evaluation.

Activity1 What's the Pattern? original Jada rule starts0 adds4, Priya rule starts0 adds8. At the same index Priya term is TWICE Jada, so Jada40 corresponds Priya80, Jada60 corresponds Priya120, and Priya192 corresponds Jada96.

Activity2 More Patterns Partner A source Jada+2 and Priya+6: Jada34 corresponds Priya102, Priya120 corresponds Jada40. Partner B source Jada+3 and Priya+9: Jada54 corresponds Priya162, Priya198 corresponds Jada66. These relationships are at the same sequence index and each begins at0.

Previously authored Rich V2 invented source A+4/B+12 and offset examples remain explicit optional Edulytiks extensions only. Original partner representation, explanation and table creation are teacher reviewed.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: generate two sequences from separate recursive rules and explain how corresponding terms relate MULTIPLICATIVELY, not only by listing numbers. The 2021 source has a relationship so a distant number such as192 can be reasoned about without extending a very long table.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: generate pairs from zero using +3 and+6: at corresponding term index n≥0 the numbers are 3n and6n. The second sequence is twice the first; every number of the second sequence appears in the first, but the reverse is not true for all terms. Keep the starting index and first term clear.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — original distant-term reasoning: from zero, pattern A adds4 and pattern B adds12. Their aligned terms are 0/0,4/12,8/24,12/36, etc.; B=3A for corresponding entries. If A reaches80, B is240. If B reaches192, A is64. Explain using the relationship rather than enumerating20 or16 terms.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — inverse relationship: choose a second pair starting at zero, adding5 and10. If the second value reaches70, the first is35. If the first reaches90, the second is180. Partners compare two legitimate explanations of why B=2A remains true for every corresponding index, and whether the same formula would hold after changing starting values.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: the source requires pattern displays, corresponding-index evidence, far-term predictions and mathematical conversation. A single numeric answer cannot certify the learner has correctly matched terms rather than merely spotting familiar factors.

KeyConcepts.Title: Recursive generation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A pattern starting 0 and adding k yields kn at step n.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiplicative correspondence
KeyConcepts.Definition: If two patterns start zero and their increments are in ratio three, corresponding values keep that ratio.

KeyConcepts.Title: Far-term prediction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use a justified relationship to calculate distant terms efficiently.
KeyConcepts.Example: No need to list every intermediate term.

Lessons.Title: More Patterns
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U07:L10 compares three PAIRS of recursively generated patterns, including starting values offset differently and fractional relationships, so corresponding terms can obey both multiplication and additive correction.
Warm-up original TRUE/FALSE276÷3=(1/3)×276 TRUE;276÷3=276/6 FALSE; (276÷3)×2=(2/3)×276 TRUE. Teacher asks equivalent operations and the fraction-of-number meaning.

Activity1 Mix and Match original SetA starts0 add3 versus starts0 add6, B=2A. SetB starts4 add3 versus starts9 add6, B=2A+1 rather than simple doubling. SetC starts0 add5 versus starts0 add3, B=3/5 A for corresponding terms. Source pupils express relationships as equations.

Activity2 Generate Patterns Partner A starts0 with+4 and+6, so first40→second60 and second120→first80. Partner B +2 and+3, so first30→second45 and second60→first40. No unstated offset may be invented for either starting-zero pair.

Correct prior fictional sets with different step sizes stay optional Edulytiks examples but are not printed source. Teacher reviews tables, relationships in words and justifications; exact chosen calculations are a bounded subset.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: compare multiple pairs of recursive number patterns, including cases whose corresponding terms are NOT simple multiples because starting values differ. The source first presents three pattern pairs and asks for any valid relationships; later returns to clear ratios like3/2.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: contrast A starting0 adding3 and B starting0 adding6: B=2A. Compare another pair A starting4 adding3, B starting9 adding6: corresponding values satisfy B=2A+1, not B=2A. Emphasize the extra offset due to different starting values.

Activity1 Heads or Tails original Han/Jada flip results are shown in a publisher-only image; pupil must read actual plotted points, then flip a coin TEN times and record own (heads,tails) where x counts heads, y counts tails and x+y=10. The results are nondeterministic and never fabricated in this source-aligned record.

Activity2 Coin Values original chart x number of coins, y total value in CENTS. Tyler has1 dime+3 nickels+2 pennies=6 coins and27c →(6,27). Lin has3 quarters+1 dime+1 penny=5 coins and86c →(5,86). Diego has1 quarter+1 dime=(2,35). Clare five coins with NO quarter corresponds (5,18) from the original plotted values; one candidate composition is1 dime+1 nickel+3 pennies.

Points (0,10),(3,7),(5,5),(10,0) have different coordinates but all represent ten outcomes. This is a deterministic relationship for counts, not a prediction that real flips must be evenly split.

Mark these points with x=heads and y=tails. When two pupils report (6,4), use distinct names or a count marker at same point; one coordinate pair can represent multiple observations.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — coin collection graph: x-axis number of coins and y-axis total value in cents. For a set of2 dimes,3 nickels,1 penny, x=6 and y=20+15+1=36 cents, point (6,36). For3 quarters and1 nickel, x=4 and y=75+5=80 cents, point (4,80). Explain why two different coin collections can have equal counts but different values, and why a plotted point does not tell the unique composition without additional information.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: the source asks for plotted coordinates and their real-unit meanings, repeated outcomes and contextual inference. Teacher inspects coordinate charts, units and interpretation; numeric coin totals alone are not evidence of a completed graph.

KeyConcepts.Definition: For exactly ten independent coin flips counted as heads or tails, H+T=10.
KeyConcepts.Rule: (6,4) is valid; (6,5) is not for ten flips.

KeyConcepts.Title: Count vs value
KeyConcepts.Definition: Number of coins alone does not determine their monetary total.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Six coins can represent many cent totals.

Lessons.Title: Patterns in the Coordinate Plane
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U07:L13 creates and GRAPHS ordered pairs (length,width) of rectangles under fixed PERIMETER12cm versus fixed AREA16cm². Different numerical constraints produce different graph shapes.

Warm-up Estimation Exploration Window Washing asks one window's area from an original CC0 Unsplash photo, but without verified physical dimensions no exact area can be read from the picture; pupil estimates are teacher scored.

Activity1 Rectangle Perimeters original Jada perimeter12cm, so length+width=6cm and width=6−length; source square is3×3cm, if length2.5 width3.5, if length3.25 width2.75. Students complete source table and DRAW graph points rather than only calculating.

Activity2 Rectangle Areas original area16cm², so width=16/length; for length5cm width3.2, length3cm width16/3, and original square4×4. Graphing length and width shows multiplicative rather than additive relation. Positive dimensions required.

Prior invented perimeter16/area12 examples in Rich V2 are independent Edulytiks exercises only. The source graph, CC0 photo, estimate, original plot and written explanations remain teacher reviewed, while selected Practice handles bounded numeric computations.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: connect fixed PERIMETER versus fixed AREA rectangles to different relationships between length and width, and plot the resulting ordered pairs. The source specifically contrasts addition-based perimeter with multiplication-based area and allows fractional or decimal side lengths.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: a rectangle of perimeter16cm satisfies length+width=8cm. Possible pairs (1,7),(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3) lie on a descending straight line. Ask learners to explain why one side growing by1 forces the other to shrink by1.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — constant perimeter: choose a perimeter of16cm. Length x and width y satisfy2x+2y=16, or y=8−x. For length2.5cm width5.5cm, and length3.25cm width4.75cm. Both give perimeter16cm. Plot and label the positions with a scale allowing quarters, explaining why two side lengths must remain positive.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — constant area: choose area12cm². Then length×width=12, so examples (1,12),(2,6),(3,4),(4,3) fit, and (5,2.4) also fits. Compare this curved decreasing relationship with the straight fixed-perimeter line. A square with area12 requires each side √12cm, not a convenient whole length; a teacher may accept an approximate value with justification, but avoid claiming a rational integer exact side.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: source requires constructing tables, plotting fractional coordinates and interpreting the TWO different constraints. Equal perimeter does not imply equal area; numeric products alone cannot verify a coordinate plot or discussion of why the patterns differ.

KeyConcepts.Title: Perimeter fixes a sum
KeyConcepts.Definition: For perimeter P, length+width=P/2.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use x+y=area to find a constant-area width
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area is a product of perpendicular lengths, not their sum.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use xy=A for area, x+y=P/2 for perimeter.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume two rectangles of same perimeter must have same area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Multiple length-width pairs share a perimeter but have different products.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare (3,5) with (4,4), both P16 but areas15 and16.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use unrelated or invented examples rather than the actual source pattern rules and plotted values.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original IM2021 printed student activities use specific decimal values and require place-value reasoning, so substituting unrelated examples or accepting a right-justified digit alignment does not preserve source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore the exact source pattern, coin, and rectangle constants; preserve open plotting and story decisions as teacher-scored.
